how-to-block-or-allow-ai-crawlers.html.text:
← Back to AI Crawler Access Check

Exact robots.txt lines for each named AI crawler

Each block below is a complete, self-contained robots.txt group. Stack as many as you need in the same file. A crawler that matches a named group ignores your wildcard (User-agent: *) group entirely — the most specific matching group wins, groups are never combined.

Block a crawler entirely

User-agent: GPTBot
Disallow: /

Swap in any token from the table below. To block several with the same rule, list them as consecutive User-agent lines before the shared Disallow:

User-agent: GPTBot
User-agent: Google-Extended
User-agent: CCBot
Disallow: /

Explicitly allow a crawler even when your wildcard group blocks everything

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

User-agent: ClaudeBot
Allow: /

Known AI crawler tokens

TokenOperatorPurpose
GPTBotOpenAITraining
ChatGPT-UserOpenAIFetches on behalf of a live ChatGPT user
OAI-SearchBotOpenAIChatGPT search index
ClaudeBotAnthropicTraining
Claude-UserAnthropicFetches on behalf of a live Claude user
Claude-SearchBotAnthropicClaude search/citation index
Google-ExtendedGoogleGemini/Vertex AI training & grounding (not Search indexing)
Applebot-ExtendedAppleApple Intelligence training (not Siri/Spotlight indexing)
CCBotCommon Crawl FoundationGeneral web archive, widely used as a training input
PerplexityBotPerplexitySearch/answer index
Perplexity-UserPerplexityFetches on behalf of a live user query
BytespiderByteDanceTraining
AmazonbotAmazonProduct/service improvement, including AI features
Meta-ExternalAgentMetaTraining & search features
Meta-ExternalFetcherMetaUser-initiated fetches
DiffbotDiffbotCommercial extraction, resold as a data feed

This list is a snapshot summarized from public reporting and each operator's own documentation — operators add crawlers and change stated purposes over time. Check the AI Crawler Access Check tool against your current robots.txt, and confirm anything load-bearing directly with the operator.

What llms.txt is (and isn't)

llms.txt is an emerging, optional convention for a plain-text file at /llms.txt: an H1 title, an optional one-line blockquote summary, and Markdown-linked sections pointing an AI assistant at your most important pages. It is not a standard any crawler is documented to require, and it does not control crawling — robots.txt still does that. A minimal one looks like this:

# Your Site

> One sentence describing what this site is.

## Docs
- [Getting started](https://example.com/docs/start)
- [API reference](https://example.com/docs/api)

The AI Crawler Access Check tool checks the basic shape above and flags what's missing.

Common questions

How do I block GPTBot (OpenAI) from crawling my site?

Add a dedicated group to robots.txt: "User-agent: GPTBot" followed by "Disallow: /". A wildcard "User-agent: *" block does not cover GPTBot if a more specific GPTBot group also exists — the most specific matching group wins, not the sum of both.

How do I block every AI crawler at once?

There is no single standard token meaning "all AI crawlers" — each operator uses its own token. The reliable way is one Disallow: / group per named token you want blocked, or a broad "User-agent: *" / "Disallow: /" block if you intend to block all automated crawling, AI or not, which will also stop most search-engine indexing.

Does Google-Extended block Google Search from indexing my site?

No. Google-Extended controls only whether Google's generative-AI products (Gemini, Vertex AI) may use the content for training and grounding. Blocking it does not affect Googlebot or normal Search indexing, which is a separate user-agent.

What's the difference between GPTBot and ChatGPT-User?

GPTBot crawls to train OpenAI's models. ChatGPT-User fetches a specific page because a live ChatGPT user's session asked it to (browsing, plugins, actions). Blocking one does not block the other, and many sites intentionally allow ChatGPT-User while blocking GPTBot.

Do I need an llms.txt file?

No — it's an optional, emerging convention (see llmstxt.org), not a standard any crawler is documented to require. It's a plain-text file at /llms.txt giving an AI assistant a short map of your key pages: an H1 title, an optional one-line summary, and Markdown link sections.

No warranty. This page is informational, provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. Crawler tokens, stated purposes, and behavior change over time — verify anything load-bearing directly with the operator's own current documentation before relying on it.

AI CRAWLER ACCESS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Which AI crawlers can actually read your site?

Paste your robots.txt and this checks it against 20 named AI-crawler user-agents — GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, and more — so you can see in one place who's allowed in, who's blocked, and who falls through to your wildcard rule by accident.

Nothing is uploaded. The text you paste is parsed in this browser and never leaves your device.

1. Try fetching it automatically, or paste it

2. Crawler-by-crawler verdict

CrawlerOperatorPurposeStatusMatched rule

Prefer a CLI, or want this as a CI gate?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file — and it can fetch a live domain directly (Node has no cross-origin restriction, unlike this page):

node cli.mjs example.com                         # human-readable report
node cli.mjs example.com --json                   # machine-readable
node cli.mjs example.com --fail-if-blocked GPTBot,ClaudeBot
node cli.mjs example.com --fail-if-allowed Bytespider
node cli.mjs --robots-file ./robots.txt --llms-file ./llms.txt

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install. It only talks to the domain you name (or reads local files) and makes no other network call.

Common questions

Which AI crawlers does this check?

A curated list of 20 named user-agent tokens publicly documented by their operators: GPTBot, ChatGPT-User and OAI-SearchBot (OpenAI); ClaudeBot, Claude-User and Claude-SearchBot (Anthropic); Google-Extended (Google); Applebot-Extended (Apple); CCBot (Common Crawl); PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User (Perplexity); Bytespider (ByteDance); Amazonbot (Amazon); Meta-ExternalAgent, Meta-ExternalFetcher and FacebookBot (Meta); DuckAssistBot (DuckDuckGo); MistralAI-User (Mistral AI); Google-CloudVertexBot (Google); and Diffbot. It's a snapshot, not a live feed — operators add crawlers and change stated purposes over time, so verify anything load-bearing directly with the operator.

Does blocking a crawler here mean it actually obeys robots.txt?

No. robots.txt is a request, not an enforcement mechanism, and this tool only reports what your file says. Reputable operators state that they honor it for the tokens listed here, but nothing stops a request that lies about its own user-agent, and robots.txt cannot verify who is really asking.

What does "partially blocked" mean?

The crawler is allowed on some of the paths checked and blocked on others — most often because it falls through to your wildcard (User-agent: *) group, which usually blocks more than the root path.

Is my robots.txt uploaded anywhere?

No. The browser page parses the text you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere. The CLI fetches only the domain you name, or reads a local file.

What is llms.txt?

An emerging, optional convention (see llmstxt.org) for a plain-text file at /llms.txt that gives an AI assistant a short, structured map of a site's key pages. This tool checks the basic shape the convention describes — an H1 title, an optional summary, and Markdown link sections — not full spec conformance.

More: exact robots.txt lines to block or allow each AI crawler, and what llms.txt is for.

Already using (or considering) a hosted, account-based service for this? See this tool vs. Known Agents (formerly Dark Visitors).

Usually check each crawler operator's own docs page by hand instead? See this tool vs. checking each crawler's docs page by hand.

Don't have an llms.txt yet, or want one built from your docs instead of hand-written? llms.txt Generator builds a spec-compliant one from a pasted page list, a sitemap.xml, or a local Markdown docs tree — the complementary job to this page's structural check.

vs-checking-each-crawlers-docs-by-hand.h.text:
← Back to AI Crawler Access Check

This tool vs. checking each crawler's docs page by hand

Names no specific company or product -- this compares against the manual habit most site owners already have: open each AI-crawler operator's own docs page one at a time (OpenAI's, Anthropic's, Google's, Apple's, Perplexity's, and five more), note the user-agent token it names, and cross-reference that token against your own robots.txt by eye.

What checking the docs pages by hand actually does

Reading each operator's own documentation is free and needs no tool, and it is the authoritative source -- this tool's own token list is sourced from exactly those pages. That method has failure modes specific to this domain that this tool exists to close. First, there are twelve separate operators publishing twenty tokens between them, in twelve different documentation formats, and a manual pass that skips one operator silently skips every token that operator controls -- Diffbot, Amazonbot, Meta-ExternalAgent, CCBot and the training-specific Applebot-Extended are each easy to miss next to the well-known GPTBot. Second, the actual effect of a robots.txt file is not "the first matching rule wins", which is how a list of rules reads to most people skimming top to bottom -- it is a longest-matching-path-wins algorithm, ties going to Allow, the same one Google documents for its own crawlers. Reproducing that correctly by eye, across every group in a file, is exactly the kind of mechanical step a person skims past. Third, several operators split one company's crawling into two or three tokens with different purposes -- training, user-initiated browsing, and search-index retrieval -- and blocking the training token does nothing to the other two, a routine manual mistake when only one of an operator's docs pages gets read. Fourth, a by-hand check leaves nothing behind afterward: no file, no per-token verdict, no audit trail, only a recollection that someone looked.

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Confirm exactly what one operator states its crawler does, in its own words, as the authoritative source. That operator's own docs page -- this tool's token list is sourced from exactly those pages and is not a substitute for reading them directly.
Check your existing robots.txt against all 20 named tokens across all twelve operators at once, without opening twelve separate docs pages. This tool -- paste your file and get every token's current status in one pass.
Apply the longest-match-wins, ties-to-Allow algorithm correctly, instead of reading rules top to bottom as if the first match wins. This tool -- it implements the documented algorithm mechanically, the same way for every group in the file.
See whether blocking one of an operator's tokens (say, GPTBot) leaves that operator's other tokens (ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot) allowed. This tool -- each token is reported separately, with its purpose, so a training block and a user-browsing allow do not get conflated.
Add a CI gate that fails a build the moment a specific crawler becomes allowed again after someone edits the file. This tool's CLI -- node cli.mjs example.com --fail-if-allowed GPTBot, no account needed.
Keep a record you can paste into a PR description or an audit trail: every token, and its current allowed/blocked/partial status. This tool -- --json gives a machine-readable version of the same report.

Checking the docs by hand is not wrong so much as unverifiable and easy to apply inconsistently: someone who reads all twelve operators' pages, remembers every token, and correctly reproduces the longest-match algorithm by eye would eventually reach the same answer this tool gives. What that method structurally cannot do is guarantee the same twelve pages get re-checked every time the file changes, or leave behind anything but a memory that someone looked -- which is what this tool's fixed token list and deterministic report exist to replace, for free.

Common questions

What does opening each crawler operator's docs page actually catch?

It catches whatever tokens you already knew to look for and remembered to check. GPTBot is well known; Diffbot, Amazonbot, Meta-ExternalAgent, CCBot and Applebot-Extended (a separate token from the regular Applebot that has crawled the web for search since long before AI training was a question) are each documented on a different operator's own site, in a different format, and a manual pass that skips one of the twelve operators silently skips every token that operator publishes.

Why is reading robots.txt by eye risky even once you have the full token list?

Because the actual effect of a robots.txt file is not "the first matching rule wins", which is how most people read a list of rules top to bottom. Google documents, and most major crawlers follow, a longest-matching-path-wins algorithm where ties go to Allow -- so a broad wildcard Disallow block followed later by a narrower Allow for one token does not mean the wildcard rule applies to that token first. Reproducing that algorithm correctly by eye, across every group in a file, is exactly the kind of mechanical step a person skims past.

Does blocking one bot from an operator block that operator's other bots too?

No, and this is a common manual mistake. OpenAI alone publishes three separate tokens with three different purposes -- GPTBot for model training, ChatGPT-User for fetching a page because a ChatGPT user's session asked it to, and OAI-SearchBot for building ChatGPT's search results -- and Anthropic and Perplexity each split the same way. Blocking GPTBot to opt out of training does nothing to ChatGPT-User or OAI-SearchBot; a robots.txt written by someone who only checked one of an operator's docs pages routinely blocks or allows the wrong one of the three.

Can I paste a note in a PR description saying I checked the docs pages by hand?

Only as a note that someone looked and did not personally notice a problem -- it names no specific token, no specific line of the file, and no verdict, so there is nothing to attach to an audit trail besides recollection. A structured report naming all 20 tokens and their current allowed/blocked/partial status is stronger evidence than "I checked the docs and it looked right."

vs-known-agents.html.text:
← Back to AI Crawler Access Check

This tool vs. Known Agents

Known Agents (renamed from Dark Visitors in early 2026 -- the old darkvisitors.com domain now redirects to it) is a hosted, account-based service built around a continuously updated directory of AI agents, crawlers and bots. Per its own site and its WordPress plugin listing, it generates and keeps a site's robots.txt current against that directory as new agents appear, can block scrapers that ignore robots.txt, and reports analytics on bot traffic and AI-referral traffic -- visits arriving from ChatGPT, Perplexity and similar -- over time. It ships as a WordPress plugin and an install for other stacks, and needs an account.

This tool is a different shape entirely: a free, static page -- and a zero-dependency Node CLI -- that reads the robots.txt and llms.txt text you already have, pasted or fetched, against a fixed, publicly documented list of 20 named AI-crawler tokens (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot and 11 more), and reports right now, deterministically, which are allowed, blocked, or partially blocked. It writes nothing, maintains nothing, tracks no traffic, and needs no account or install.

Which one answers your question

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Keep a robots.txt current against a continuously updated directory of AI agents, without editing it by hand as new ones appear. Known Agents -- an auto-updating, managed robots.txt is its core feature.
See an analytics dashboard of bot traffic and AI-referral visits (ChatGPT, Perplexity) hitting your site over time. Known Agents -- this tool reports nothing about traffic, only what a file currently says.
Check, right now, exactly what your existing robots.txt allows or blocks for 20 named AI crawlers, with no account and nothing installed. This tool -- paste the file and get a deterministic verdict in your browser.
Add a CI gate that fails a build the moment GPTBot (or any named crawler) becomes allowed again. This tool's CLI -- node cli.mjs example.com --fail-if-allowed GPTBot, no account needed.
Actively block scrapers that ignore robots.txt entirely, not just report what the file says. Known Agents' blocking feature, per its own listing -- this tool never blocks anything; it only reads and reports.
Audit a robots.txt you inherited or just wrote, once, with nothing left running afterward. This tool -- it is a check, not a service you install and maintain.

These are complementary rather than competing: a site running Known Agents for an auto-updating file and traffic analytics can still use this tool to independently verify, with no account and no trust in a third-party dashboard, exactly what the resulting robots.txt allows right now -- and a site that wants no ongoing service at all can use this tool alone as a one-time or CI-gated check.

Common questions

Should I use this checker or Known Agents?

They are different shapes of tool and plenty of sites end up using both. Known Agents (formerly Dark Visitors, at knownagents.com) is a hosted, account-based service built around a continuously updated directory of AI agents, crawlers and bots; per its own site and WordPress plugin listing it can generate and keep a site's robots.txt current against that directory, block scrapers that ignore robots.txt, and report analytics on bot traffic and AI-referral traffic (from ChatGPT, Perplexity and similar) over time. This tool does none of that. It is a free, static page (and a zero-dependency Node CLI) that reads the robots.txt and llms.txt text you already have -- pasted, fetched, or read from disk -- against a fixed, publicly documented list of 20 named AI-crawler tokens, and reports right now, deterministically, which are allowed, blocked, or partially blocked. Reach for Known Agents if you want an ongoing, managed directory and a traffic dashboard. Reach for this tool for an immediate, no-account read of the file you already have, or to wire a CI gate around it.

Does this replace Known Agents' auto-updating robots.txt?

No, and it is not trying to. Known Agents' core feature, per its own documentation, is generating and maintaining a robots.txt against its own continuously updated agent directory, so a site's file stays current as new crawlers appear without anyone editing it by hand. This tool never writes or maintains a file -- it only reads whatever robots.txt you give it, against a fixed snapshot of 20 named tokens, and tells you what that file currently does. If you want a robots.txt that updates itself as new AI agents launch, that is Known Agents' job, not this tool's. If you want to check, right now, exactly what an existing file allows or blocks -- your own, or one you inherited -- that is this tool's job.

Is my data uploaded anywhere, the way an analytics dashboard would collect it?

Not by this tool. The browser page parses the robots.txt/llms.txt text you paste entirely in your own browser and never sends it anywhere; the CLI only ever contacts the one domain you name, to fetch its robots.txt and llms.txt, and makes no other network call. It keeps no traffic log and has no dashboard -- it reports the current file's rules and nothing about who visits your site. Known Agents' analytics dashboard is a different kind of product: reporting ongoing bot and AI-referral traffic necessarily means it observes requests hitting your site over time, which this tool never does.

Is this page affiliated with Known Agents or Dark Visitors?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Known Agents (formerly Dark Visitors) or its operators. Known Agents and Dark Visitors are named here only to describe what this tool is and is not, based on Known Agents' own public site and WordPress plugin listing; check those for what the service currently offers and how.
